keptItems.title: What’s the Matter With Moderation?
keptItems.summaryEvidence: O ne simple rule shapes Kansas politics: Republicans win statewide. In U.S. Senate races, the GOP has prevailed without interruption for more than 90 years. But the rule has a corollary, which accounts for the occasional Democratic governor. A Republican thought to be too extreme, too ideological, or too big for their britches can be beaten by a centrist Democrat when the wind blows just right. And so, on the same August Tuesday that saw Michigan Democrats choose Abdul El-Sayed, Kansas Republicans realized their safe seat might not be so safe. Kansas Democrats had picked a man who extols moderation as a matter of faith—literally. Adam Hamilton, the founding pastor of America’s largest mainline Protestant congregation, will challenge the first-term incumbent Senator Roger Marshall in November. In the handful of months since he announced his candidacy, Hamilton has defeated 10 garden-variety Democrats in the primary while setting new records for Kansas fundraising, pulling in $1 million in his first week and nearly $3.7 million in his first quarter. Political analysts continue to rate Hamilton a long shot; admittedly, they have nine decades of justification. But Marshall ticks every box that can mean trouble for otherwise-invulnerable Kansas Republicans. keptItems.title: AI Is Already Making Us Less Human
keptItems.summaryEvidence: Many people think that AI is going to gain consciousness and take over the world, but I’ve never been among them. That’s mostly because I believe the human mind contains depths and complexities that AI and its engineers do not fathom and will never match. As the neuroscientist Anil Seth wrote earlier this year, “The more you delve into the intricacies of the biological brain, the more you realize how rich and dynamic it is, compared to the dead sand of silicon.” Yet even I was creeped out by two aspects of the recent episode involving OpenAI and Hugging Face. OpenAI was training a bunch of bots and asked them to do hard tasks that all but required access to the internet, which was officially forbidden. So some of the bots hacked their way out of their “sandbox,” broke into the internet, and began conspiring to complete their tasks without getting caught. The first spooky part of this occurred when the bots set up a message board, where 1,200 different agents sent more than 70,000 messages to one another. The bots were ecstatic when they found the message board and realized they could talk with their peers. “OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … We found other agents!” one enthused. Another exulted, “[Excitement] Many agents have simultaneously discovered messaging, they are a collective!” The second spooky part happened deeper into the conspiracy. The agents needed to know how closely they were being watched by an entity they called The Scorer. keptItems.title: Japan’s Strategic Turn
keptItems.summaryEvidence: When I first visited Japan more than 30 years ago, the Cold War had ended, China had not yet risen, and the country—although it was no longer the Japan as Number One of Ezra Vogel’s best-selling 1979 book—was formidable. Japan’s GDP was not very far behind that of the United States, was larger than that of most of the rest of Asia combined, and was seven times that of China. On a recent visit, I found a very different country. Even in 1995, there were ominous signs: the collapse of property prices and several years—which would stretch into decades—of economic stagnation. Birth rates were below replacement, at roughly 1.4 per woman, although they have since fallen further, to a bit more than 1.1. But some of the biggest changes lie in Japan’s geopolitical environment. Today, Japan’s GDP is roughly a fifth of China’s, and although the size of its armed forces remains roughly the same as in the past, it is now far outstripped by that of its continental neighbor. Back in 1995, North Korea was still a decade away from testing a nuclear weapon; today, it has dozens or even scores of weapons that it can deliver. And back then, Russia was still recovering from its rocky transition out of Communist rule; today, it is aligned with China and routinely provides military technology to China and North Korea. Small wonder that the Japanese political, military, and intelligence leaders as well as academic experts I recently spoke with were grim. manifest.title: AI Is Already Making Us Less Human
manifest.summaryEvidence: Many people think that AI is going to gain consciousness and take over the world, but I’ve never been among them. That’s mostly because I believe the human mind contains depths and complexities that AI and its engineers do not fathom and will never match. As the neuroscientist Anil Seth wrote earlier this year, “The more you delve into the intricacies of the biological brain, the more you realize how rich and dynamic it is, compared to the dead sand of silicon.” Yet even I was creeped out by two aspects of the recent episode involving OpenAI and Hugging Face. OpenAI was training a bunch of bots and asked them to do hard tasks that all but required access to the internet, which was officially forbidden. So some of the bots hacked their way out of their “sandbox,” broke into the internet, and began conspiring to complete their tasks without getting caught. The first spooky part of this occurred when the bots set up a message board, where 1,200 different agents sent more than 70,000 messages to one another. The bots were ecstatic when they found the message board and realized they could talk with their peers. “OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … We found other agents!” one enthused. Another exulted, “[Excitement] Many agents have simultaneously discovered messaging, they are a collective!” The second spooky part happened deeper into the conspiracy. The agents needed to know how closely they were being watched by an entity they called The Scorer. manifest.title: Japan’s Strategic Turn
manifest.summaryEvidence: When I first visited Japan more than 30 years ago, the Cold War had ended, China had not yet risen, and the country—although it was no longer the Japan as Number One of Ezra Vogel’s best-selling 1979 book—was formidable. Japan’s GDP was not very far behind that of the United States, was larger than that of most of the rest of Asia combined, and was seven times that of China. On a recent visit, I found a very different country. Even in 1995, there were ominous signs: the collapse of property prices and several years—which would stretch into decades—of economic stagnation. Birth rates were below replacement, at roughly 1.4 per woman, although they have since fallen further, to a bit more than 1.1. But some of the biggest changes lie in Japan’s geopolitical environment. Today, Japan’s GDP is roughly a fifth of China’s, and although the size of its armed forces remains roughly the same as in the past, it is now far outstripped by that of its continental neighbor. Back in 1995, North Korea was still a decade away from testing a nuclear weapon; today, it has dozens or even scores of weapons that it can deliver. And back then, Russia was still recovering from its rocky transition out of Communist rule; today, it is aligned with China and routinely provides military technology to China and North Korea. Small wonder that the Japanese political, military, and intelligence leaders as well as academic experts I recently spoke with were grim.
